summary: Specifies the Authentication-Results message header field, which records the results of message authentication efforts so mail filters and mail clients can use them. It obsoletes RFC 7601 and is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: A stamp on an email that says which security checks it passed or failed, so later programs can decide what to do.

questions: spf dkim dmarc results in headers
how to read authentication-results spf dkim
subtitle: A mail header that records which authentication checks a message passed or failed, so later software can act on the results.

tldr.problem: Mail servers run checks such as DKIM and SPF, but downstream filters and mail clients need a common, machine-readable place to find the results.
tldr.mechanism: The Authentication-Results header field names the service that did the checking and lists method=result statements with the message properties used. Servers add it at the top of the message and strip look-alike copies from outside their trust boundary.
tldr.outcome: It is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 7601. A pass in the header does not by itself make a message trustworthy.

today: RFC 8601 is a Proposed Standard published in May 2019. It obsoletes RFC 7601, and its metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Record Authentication Results
sections.content:
RFC 8601 defines the Authentication-Results header field. It presents the results of message authentication in a machine-readable format, so that a Mail User Agent (MUA) and downstream filters can make filtering decisions or recommend to the user whether a message's origin is valid. End users are not expected to read it directly. The RFC also does not say what filtering decisions are appropriate or how an MUA should display results, since those are local policy and interface design questions.

The goals are to convey results from upstream filters and Mail Transfer Agents (MTAs) to MUAs and downstream filters in the same trust domain, to provide one common location for that data, and to create an extensible framework for new methods. The RFC lists the methods published at the time, including SMTP AUTH, DKIM, DMARC, SPF and its own iprev check.

The RFC adds no new requirements on existing protocols and does not require MTAs to reject messages that fail authentication. It also warns that the mere presence of the header does not mean its contents are valid.
sections.eli5: When a letter arrives, the mailroom checks a few things about it and writes the results on a sticker. Later helpers read the sticker instead of redoing the checks.

sections.title: Trust Boundaries and Roles
sections.content:
The header only makes sense inside an Administrative Management Domain (ADMD). A trust boundary separates internal services, which are under the ADMD's authority, from external ones. How trust is obtained is a local matter. A producer adds the header; a consumer parses it for handling decisions.

The RFC assumes authentication happens at a border MTA or a delivery MTA. A border MTA is the gateway between the Internet and the organization's users. A delivery MTA actually delivers the message to the user's inbox. Messages that leave and re-enter a trust boundary, such as a forwarded message attached as message/rfc822, cannot be trusted for these details, so the header found there is typically ignored.

Results are meant to say that authentication was already done inside the boundary. They are not meant to let consumers repeat the authentication themselves.
sections.eli5: The sticker is only believable if it was put on by someone in your own mailroom. A sticker that came on a letter from outside might be fake.

sections.title: The Header Field Format
sections.content:
The header is a structured trace field, added at the top of the message as it passes MTAs that do checks. Its value (after removing comments) is an authentication service identifier (authserv-id), an optional version, and then statements of the form method=result. Each statement can include a reason string and ptype.property=value items showing which message properties were evaluated. The special form none means no authentication was performed. The header can appear several times in one message, or carry several results.

A ptype says where a property came from: body, header, smtp or policy. SMTP commands are written in lowercase without spaces, so MAIL FROM becomes mailfrom. The policy ptype records a local policy decision that augments or overrides the method's result. The RFC's example is a DKIM signature that passes but does not cover the Subject field, which an ADMD may choose to report as dkim=policy policy.dkim-rules=unsigned-subject.

The authserv-id must be unique to the ADMD that generates it (MUST). It SHOULD be a common token across the ADMD, and common practice is the organization's DNS domain name. A version token lets a parser stop if it meets a version it does not know, and a method version lets a parser ignore results whose semantics it does not support.
sections.eli5: The sticker starts with who made it, then lists each check and its answer, like 'spelling: good'. A short note can say what was looked at.

sections.title: Methods and Result Values
sections.content:
Each method returns one of a set of result values. For DKIM (method dkim), the results are none, pass, fail, policy, neutral, temperror and permerror. DKIM properties use the header ptype and name tags of the DKIM-Signature field, such as header.d for the signing domain. This revision also registers the tags a (algorithm) and s (selector) as reportable.

For SPF (method spf), results are none, pass, fail, softfail, policy, neutral, temperror and permerror, reported with ptype smtp and property mailfrom or helo. For SMTP AUTH (method auth), the results are none, pass, fail, temperror and permerror, reported with smtp.auth or smtp.mailfrom.

Other registered methods include vbr, dkim-atps, dkim-adsp, rrvs and smime. New methods and results are registered with IANA and, preferably, published in an RFC. Experimental ones MUST only be used within ADMDs that agreed to use them, and production software SHOULD ignore or delete headers containing them.
sections.eli5: Each check gives a simple answer such as passed, failed, or could not tell. The sticker uses the same few answer words every time so everyone understands them.

sections.title: The iprev Method
sections.content:
This RFC defines one new method, iprev. It checks that a connecting client's IP address is tied to a domain name through DNS. The address is looked up to get names (a PTR query), then each name is looked up for A and AAAA addresses. The test succeeds if the original address appears in the resulting set.

Results are pass, fail, temperror and permerror; there is no none, since every TCP connection has an IP address. They are reported with ptype policy and property iprev. Verifiers MUST limit how many names they evaluate to avoid taxing DNS, and the RFC cites SPF's limit of 10 as an example.

The RFC is lukewarm about the method. It notes contention about its wisdom and reliability, says that reverse-mapping guidance recommends against using it for authentication or security, and describes its inclusion as an acknowledgment that the method remains common, not an endorsement.
sections.eli5: It is like calling the phone number a caller says they have, to see if it really belongs to them. It is a handy hint but not strong proof.

sections.title: Adding, Reading and Removing the Header
sections.content:
An MTA that does authentication adds the header either once per test or once for all results, and MUST NOT add a result to an existing header. It SHOULD insert the header above other trace fields it prepends. It SHOULD NOT include data that the method did not authenticate. An MTA MAY add a header with only the identifier and none to say that no authentication was done.

Consumers are cautious by design. MUAs and downstream filters SHOULD NOT interpret the header unless the user or administrator configured them to, and only for an authserv-id in use within the ADMD. They MUST ignore results with unregistered result codes, unknown ptypes or unsupported methods. MUAs SHOULD NOT show results to users without careful human-factors design, and SHOULD ignore copies inside message/rfc822 attachments.

To stop forgery, any MTA conforming to the RFC MUST delete any instance that claims, by its identifier, to have been added within its trust boundary but did not come directly from another trusted MTA. This can invalidate signatures covering the header, which the RFC calls desirable, and signers MAY omit the header from signing. Separately, if local policy rejects messages on non-recoverable failures, the border MTA SHOULD reject during the SMTP session instead of adding the header, which avoids backscatter.
sections.eli5: Each mailroom stamps its own results on top and throws away any stickers that pretend to be from its own mailroom. Readers trust a sticker only if they know the mailroom that wrote it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The main risk is forged header fields. An attacker could use a receiving ADMD's domain as the authserv-id and claim the message passed. If the MTA does not strip such headers, the MUA may trust them, so the RFC advises against enabling processing by default. It lists possible stronger fixes, such as a DKIM signature over the header, but does not mandate one and notes they have not been developed for lack of demand.

A pass also does not make mail trustworthy: spam can pass several checks, for example when signed by a spammer's own domain. Other risks include attacks against the underlying methods, DNS load from iprev queries, backscatter if rejections are not done in the SMTP session, out-of-date internal MTA lists, oversized or malformed headers aimed at parsers, and compromised internal hosts that forge both the From field and the header.
sections.eli5: Anyone can write a fake sticker, and even a real 'passed' sticker does not mean the letter is nice. So check where the sticker came from and still be careful.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
IANA registered the field in the Permanent Message Header Field Names registry, with status standard and the IETF as change controller. The RFC also restates the rules for the Email Authentication Methods, Property Types and Result Names registries. New entries need Expert Review by a designated expert appointed by the IESG, and entries can be marked active or deprecated.

This revision adds the DKIM header.a and header.s entries, updates existing entries to point to RFC 8601, and marks the sender-id method deprecated. The domainkeys and sender-id result names are also marked deprecated because they reference historic protocols.
sections.eli5: There is an official list of allowed check names and answer words. Adding a new one means getting an expert to approve it.

viz.caption: EXAMPLE 3 FROM APPENDIX B OF RFC 8601

items.label: pass
items.desc: Signed, signatures acceptable to the ADMD, and verification passed.

items.label: fail
items.desc: Signed and acceptable, but verification failed.

items.label: policy
items.desc: Signed, but some aspect was not acceptable to the ADMD.

items.label: neutral
items.desc: Signed, but with syntax errors or otherwise unprocessable.

items.label: temperror
items.desc: Likely transient error, such as being unable to fetch a public key.

items.label: permerror
items.desc: Unrecoverable error, such as a required header field being absent.

viz.caption: WHERE THE HEADER IS ADDED AND USED (RFC 8601, SECTION 1.5.4)

layers.label: Border MTA
layers.detail: Gateway to the Internet; typically applies authentication and adds the header

layers.label: Intermediate MTA
layers.detail: Passes the message along inside the trust boundary

layers.label: MDA (delivery MTA)
layers.detail: Delivers the message to the user's inbox

layers.label: MUA
layers.detail: Consumes the results if configured to do so
